analysis.one_liner: Repeals new IRS information reporting requirements for cryptocurrency transfers.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote or a single cosponsor, and the new crypto tax reporting rules stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, passed in late 2021, requires "brokers" — businesses that facilitate digital asset trades — to report customers' crypto transactions to the IRS, the same way stockbrokers report stock sales. This bill would wipe out that requirement entirely, restoring the law as if the provision had never existed, effective immediately upon enactment. It never advanced past being placed on the Senate calendar.
analysis.who_benefits: Cryptocurrency firms and active traders would gain. Exchanges, and possibly miners, stakers, and wallet or software providers who feared being swept into the definition of "broker," would be freed from new reporting and compliance obligations. Traders' crypto sales would no longer generate third-party tax forms reporting their proceeds to the IRS, making underreporting of crypto gains easier to conceal and harder for the IRS to detect.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 80603 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act in its entirety, which means the new requirement that digital asset brokers report customer transactions to the IRS would disappear, effective the day the bill is enacted.

Repealing the provision restores the pre-existing law as if the reporting mandate had never been enacted, sparing crypto businesses the cost and complexity of building new reporting systems and relieving participants in the digital asset market — including miners and validators, who do not hold customer information — from any obligation to file transaction reports.

analysis.who_pays: The IRS and honest taxpayers. Without broker reporting, the IRS loses its main window into crypto sales, so underreporting of digital asset gains becomes easier and tax collection on that wealth shifts toward people whose wages and interest are reported by employers and banks. The repeal would also erase a revenue provision that helped pay for the infrastructure law.

drawbacks.text: Wiping out all broker reporting would leave crypto gains largely invisible to the IRS, widening the gap between taxes owed and taxes collected, and shifting more of the burden onto wage earners whose income is automatically reported.

The underlying broker definition was genuinely flawed — critics argued it could sweep in miners and software developers who have no customer data and could not realistically comply — but this bill responds with blanket repeal rather than narrowing the rule, so it would also eliminate reporting that helps ordinary investors file accurate returns and that the infrastructure law counted on for revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem — the infrastructure law's definition of 'broker' was written broadly enough that miners and developers without customer records faced a mandate they could not meet — but it goes far beyond fixing that. Blanket repeal would end all third-party reporting on an asset class where underreporting is already common, handing a compliance and enforcement reprieve to the industry at the expense of tax collection from everyone else. A targeted amendment narrowing 'broker' would have addressed the flaw without discarding the enforcement tool entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but no senator ever joined it, no committee ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on November 15, 2021, to repeal the digital asset reporting provisions of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

It was read the first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar, then read a second time the next day and placed under General Orders as Calendar No. 168 — a parking spot on the calendar, not scheduled action.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, no committee was assigned, and no floor vote ever happened; the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The new reporting requirements stayed in the law, so the IRS keeps its visibility into crypto transactions and honest taxpayers are spared some of the shifted burden; the crypto industry remains subject to the reporting it sought to repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tax enforcement; crypto firms still report

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the crypto broker reporting provisions and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Cryptocurrency industry groups
for.what_they_did: Lobbied during the infrastructure debate against the broker reporting provision, arguing it was overbroad and unworkable for miners and non-custodial actors.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only sign of support was Cruz's sponsorship, with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted them from reporting customer transactions to the IRS, sparing them compliance costs while removing the third-party reporting the IRS relies on to catch unreported crypto gains. Its failure means they remain subject to the new rules.

industries.industry: Crypto miners, stakers, and wallet and software developers
industries.note: These non-custodial participants feared being treated as 'brokers' despite holding no customer information, and the bill would have relieved them entirely. Its failure leaves them dependent on Treasury guidance to clarify they are not covered.
Repeal would have ended the broker forms that document their sales to the IRS, easing both compliance and underreporting. With the bill dead, their transactions remain reportable by platforms.
